title: You’re So Good At Conversation!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore conversation analysis, a micro-level observational field that grew out of ethnomethodology and sociolinguistics at UCLA in the 1960s and 1970s. They cover its founders (Harvey Sacks, Gail Jefferson, Emanuel Schegloff), the Jefferson transcription system, early work with an emergency psychiatric hospital's phone calls, adjacency pairs and presequences, turn-taking via turn constructional units and transition relevance places, repair, gaps, overlap and interruption (including cooperative vs. intrusive types), storytelling, laminated action, conversation "families," John Heritage's work with doctors, Elizabeth Stokoe's mediation research, customer service bots, gender and interruption research, and generational changes such as the Gen Z stare. The episode ends with a listener email about orthodontics and TMJ.

entities.name: London School of Economics and Political Science

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to conversation analysis
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh open with banter about how the episode might make them self-conscious. Chuck introduces conversation analysis as an observational social science and argues that conversation is something humans do very well without realizing it.

segments.title: History: Sacks, Jefferson and Schegloff at UCLA
segments.summary: The hosts describe the roots of conversation analysis in ethnomethodology and sociolinguistics. They cover Harvey Sacks, his early work and death in 1975, his links to Erving Goffman, Gail Jefferson's transcription work and interest in laughter, and Emanuel Schegloff's later leadership at UCLA.

segments.title: Early phone call research and the Jefferson transcription method
segments.summary: Early work focused on telephone calls, such as how callers open and close them and how turns are signaled without visual cues. The Jefferson transcription method is introduced as the key tool. The hosts also note the contrast with Chomsky's universal grammar.

segments.title: Emergency psychiatric hospital phone calls and the 'huh' disruptor
segments.summary: Sacks worked with an emergency psychiatric hospital to get callers to give their names. Greeting formats affected responses, and a response like 'huh' acted as a disruptor that shifted the conversational script.

segments.title: Adjacency pairs, 'how are you' greetings and closeness
segments.summary: Sacks identified composites and adjacency pairs, where a prompt expects a limited set of responses. The hosts discuss how 'how are you' is a ritual greeting that is largely universal, and how honest answers signal closeness.

segments.title: Video recording as a breakthrough
segments.summary: Chuck notes that the arrival of affordable video recording let analysts see body language and interaction, not just voices.

segments.title: Sponsor break and tangent
segments.summary: A break with a Stuckey's-style ad riff, followed by a tangent about Matthew Modine's diary on Full Metal Jacket and putting oneself on tape for auditions.

segments.title: Method: objectivity, meaning and transcription
segments.summary: Chuck explains that conversation analysts describe patterns without theorizing motives, deriving meaning from the next speaker's response. Recordings are transcribed objectively, with ethics requiring participants to know they are being recorded.

segments.title: Turn constructional units, transition relevance places, repair and gaps
segments.summary: The hosts define turn constructional units and transition relevance places, give exceptions like taking two turns in a row, and explain repair as correcting misunderstandings. They also describe conversation gaps and ways to handle awkward pauses.

segments.title: Adjacency pairs, preferences and the cake example
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck revisit adjacency pairs and presequences, with examples such as invitation and acceptance, and joke about a mismatched reply to an offer of cake.

segments.title: Storytelling and laminated action
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how stories end with a look that asks for a response, how discourse markers link ideas, and how gestures like eye-rolling complete a spoken meaning, which they call laminated action.

segments.title: Overlap, interruption and cooperative interruption
segments.summary: Overlap is separated from interruption. Intrusive interruptions are contrasted with cooperative interruptions, such as saying 'right' or adding detail to a story.

segments.title: Interruption across cultures: New Yorkers and Japanese talk shows
segments.summary: Deborah Tannen's study of Californians, New Yorkers and a Londoner found New Yorkers overlap frequently without offense among themselves. Samoan, Japanese and Italian American patterns are mentioned, and Japanese morning TV hosts are cited as interjecting in a way that is accepted.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Short sponsor break.

segments.title: Conversation families: reconstruction, projection and moralizing
segments.summary: Conversations are grouped into families: reconstruction (sharing past events), projection (future plans), and moralizing (judging good and bad). The hosts say negative moralizing is more elaborate than positive talk, which they link to a negativity bias.

segments.title: Applications: John Heritage, mediation and customer service bots
segments.summary: Conversation analysis is used in call centers and surgical teams. John Heritage showed that doctors' question wording changes how much patients disclose. Elizabeth Stokoe found mediation clients wanted practical steps. Customer service bots are discussed, with the advice that bots should identify themselves.

segments.title: Gender and interruptions
segments.summary: Research on whether men interrupt women more gives mixed results. A 1998 meta-analysis suggested gender differences are clearer for intrusive interruptions than cooperative ones. Upbringing explanations are offered, and first-author gender in studies is noted as a factor.

segments.title: Generational differences: Gen Z stare and phone etiquette
segments.summary: The hosts discuss generational change in conversation, including the Gen Z stare and Gen Z phone greetings that skip hello.

segments.title: Teenagers, Gen X and Douglas Coupland
segments.summary: The hosts joke about talking with teenagers and adults ignoring Gen X kids. Chuck mentions Douglas Coupland's book Generation X and the hosts discuss their current reading.

segments.title: Listener mail: orthodontics and TMJ
segments.summary: A listener named Aaron writes to correct an earlier focus on appearance in the orthodontics episode, noting links between bite alignment, sleep apnea, ADHD and TMJ dysfunction, and describing his own treatment.

segments.title: Outro and sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck invites listeners to send emails, and Josh gives the show credit and directs listeners to the iHeartRadio app.
